restaurant.name: 4 Charles Prime Rib
restaurant.about: Brendan Sodikoff’s wood-paneled West Village supper club, known for salt-crusted, slow-roasted USDA Prime rib with natural jus and horseradish cream.

recipe.name: Roast Prime Rib of Beef
aliases: Prime Rib with Jus and Horseradish Cream
recipe.subtitle: Dry-brined, salt-crusted standing rib roast cooked low and slow, carved Chicago or English cut, with natural beef jus and horseradish cream
recipe.description: A three-bone standing rib roast, dry-brined for up to three days, packed in a herb-and-egg-white salt crust and roasted at 110°C until it is rosy from edge to edge, then rested and blasted to crisp the fat. It is carved thick (Chicago) or thin (English) and served with a flour-free jus from roasted bones and a sharp, fresh horseradish cream.

items.item: bone-in standing rib roast, 3 bones, first cut (small end, ribs 10–12), USDA Prime or high Choice (6½ lb); ask the butcher to cut the bones off and tie them back on
fine sea salt, about 0.8% of the roast’s weight (4 tsp; or 3 tbsp Diamond Crystal kosher salt)
coarse kosher salt (about 3 cups Morton kosher; 1⅔ lb)
Leaves from 2 rosemary sprigs and 4 thyme sprigs, chopped
meaty beef bones, such as short rib, oxtail or neck, plus any trim from the roast (2½ lb)
large yellow onion, halved, skin on
low-sodium beef stock, ideally homemade (6⅓ cups)
4 thyme sprigs, 1 bay leaf, 8 black peppercorns
fresh horseradish root, peeled and finely grated on a Microplane (about ½ cup lightly packed)
Flaky sea salt and freshly cracked black pepper

equipment: Heavy roasting pan with a V-rack or flat rack
Rimmed baking sheet with a wire rack, for dry-brining
Leave-in probe thermometer with an alarm (essential) and an instant-read thermometer
Long, sharp slicing knife and carving board with a juice groove
Small hammer or the back of a heavy knife, to crack the crust

steps.title: Choose and prepare the roast
steps.text: Buy a 3-bone roast from the small (loin) end, ribs 10–12, sometimes labeled first cut. Ask the butcher to remove the bones in one piece and tie them back on with twine between each bone; leave about 6 mm (¼ in) of fat on the cap. If you do it yourself, run a boning knife along the bones, keep the bones, and tie them back tightly.
steps.cue: A compact roast with a large central eye and a thin, even fat cap. The bones still insulate the meat and flavor it while it roasts, but you can untie them for clean carving. Prime grade has more marbling; a well-marbled high Choice is very good with this method. “Prime rib” is the cut’s name, not a guarantee of USDA Prime grade.

steps.title: Dry-brine, uncovered
steps.text: 1–3 days ahead, pat the roast dry and season every surface, including between the bones and meat, with 24 g fine salt and the cracked pepper. Set it on a rack over a baking sheet and refrigerate, uncovered, for 24–72 hours.
steps.cue: The surface turns dry, darker and slightly tacky as the salt dissolves, is reabsorbed and travels inward. After 48 hours the outer centimeter is seasoned through. This, not the salt crust, does the real seasoning.

steps.title: Roast the bones for the jus
steps.text: On the morning you cook (or up to 4 days ahead), heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the beef bones and trim with the oil in a roasting pan and roast 25 minutes. Add the onion, carrot, celery and garlic, smear the tomato paste over the bones, and roast 20 minutes more.
steps.cue: Bones and vegetables deep brown with dark, sticky juices on the pan, but nothing black. Burnt bits make the jus bitter, so pull out anything scorched.

steps.title: Simmer and reduce the jus
steps.text: Transfer the bones and vegetables to the stockpot. Pour off the fat from the pan, set it over medium heat, add the wine (or 150 ml of the water) and scrape up every browned bit; pour it into the pot. Add the stock, water, thyme, bay and peppercorns. Bring just to a simmer, skim, and cook at a lazy simmer, uncovered, for 2 hours, skimming every 20 minutes. Strain through the fine sieve, defat, and simmer in a clean saucepan until reduced to about 600 ml (2½ cups). Don’t salt yet.
steps.cue: A clear, mahogany jus that lightly coats a spoon without being sticky or gluey. Never boil it hard: boiling emulsifies the fat into the liquid and clouds it. If it tastes thin, reduce it further; there is no flour or starch, so body comes only from reduction and gelatin.

steps.title: Bring the roast out and heat the oven
steps.text: Take the roast out of the refrigerator 1 hour before roasting. Heat the oven to 110°C (225°F); check it with an oven thermometer, since many ovens are inaccurate at low settings.
steps.cue: The surface is dry to the touch. Taking the chill off shortens the roasting time a little and helps it cook evenly.

steps.title: Make the salt crust
steps.text: In a bowl, whisk the egg whites and water until frothy, then mix in the coarse salt, cracked peppercorns and chopped herbs with your hands.
steps.cue: The texture of damp sand that holds together when squeezed. Too dry and it won’t stick; too wet and it slides — add salt or a splash of water to adjust.

steps.title: Pack the crust onto the roast
steps.text: Set the roast bone side down on the rack in the roasting pan. Insert the probe thermometer horizontally into the center of the eye from one cut end. Pack the salt mixture firmly over the fat cap and the long rounded side in an even layer about 1 cm (⅜ in) thick, leaving the two cut faces and the bones uncovered.
steps.cue: A snug, even shell with no thin spots. Leaving the cut faces open lets them brown and drip a little for the jus, and stops the ends from being over-salted.

steps.title: Roast low and slow
steps.text: Roast at 110°C (225°F) until the probe reads 50°C (122°F) for medium-rare, about 4–5 hours for a 3 kg roast (see the chef notes for other doneness levels). Set the probe alarm 3°C below the target and check it with the instant-read thermometer in two other spots before you pull it.
steps.cue: A hard, pale, set crust and a gentle sizzle from the exposed ends. Time is only a guide: a roast’s shape and your oven matter more than its weight. If it is racing ahead, lower the oven to 95°C (200°F); if it is slow, be patient rather than turning the heat up.

steps.title: Make the horseradish cream
steps.text: While the roast cooks, grate the horseradish into a bowl (open a window — the fumes are strong), wait 2 minutes, then stir in the vinegar, salt and sugar. Fold in the crème fraîche and chives and refrigerate at least 30 minutes.
steps.cue: A thick, spoonable cream with a clean, nose-clearing heat. The pungency develops in the first minutes after grating; the vinegar fixes it at that level. For a milder cream, add the vinegar immediately after grating.

steps.title: Crack off the crust and rest
steps.text: Take the roast out and turn the oven to its highest setting, 260–290°C (500–550°F). Crack the crust with a small hammer or the back of a heavy knife and lift it away in pieces. Brush off any loose salt with a pastry brush. Rest the roast on the rack, loosely tented with foil, 30–60 minutes.
steps.cue: The internal temperature climbs only 1–3°C during the rest, because the low oven leaves little heat stored at the surface. The fat cap under the crust will look pale and damp; the next step fixes that.

steps.title: Blast the fat cap
steps.text: Remove the foil and put the roast back in the very hot oven for 6–10 minutes, until the fat cap is browned and sizzling. Meanwhile, pour the drippings from the pan into a fat separator.
steps.cue: A crisp, golden-brown, crackling exterior with no gray band beneath it. Watch it closely: herbs and salt residue can scorch after 10 minutes. Because the roast has already rested, it can be carved straight away.

steps.title: Finish the jus
steps.text: Bring the reduced jus to a simmer, add the defatted roast drippings and any juices from the carving board, then season with salt a pinch at a time until savory and full but not salty (usually 1–3 g). Keep hot.
steps.cue: A glossy, deeply beefy jus. Taste it on a scrap of the roast, which is itself seasoned, before adding more salt.

steps.title: Carve Chicago or English
steps.text: Snip the twine and lift off the bones. For a Chicago cut, slice the roast into 3–4 cm (1¼–1½ in) slabs, about 450 g (1 lb) each, and serve some on the bone by cutting between the ribs. For an English cut, slice the boneless roast across the grain into thin 5 mm (scant ¼ in) slices and fan 3–4 on each plate.
steps.cue: Rosy pink from edge to edge with only a hairline band of brown under the crust, and juices that stay in the meat rather than flooding the board. Use long, single strokes of the knife rather than sawing.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Sprinkle the cut faces with flaky salt and cracked pepper. Spoon hot jus over and around the meat on warm plates and serve the horseradish cream on the side.
steps.cue: Hot jus against rosy beef, with a cool, sharp spoonful of horseradish cream for contrast.

chefNotes: **Pull temperatures (at 110°C):** rare 46°C (115°F), medium-rare 50°C (122°F), medium 54°C (130°F). After resting and the final blast, expect about 3–4°C more.

**Dry brine versus salt crust, honestly.** The dry brine does the seasoning; the crust mostly changes the cooking. It insulates the surface and traps moisture, so the outer layer cooks more gently and stays juicy, but it also prevents browning, which is why the roast needs a final blast. If you skip the crust, the dry-brined roast still works beautifully.
**Bones off and tied back** give you the insulation and flavor of a bone-in roast with the clean carving of a boneless one; the bones can be served as a cook’s treat or carved into the Chicago cut.
**A probe thermometer is not optional.** At 110°C there is a wide window, but only the internal temperature tells you where you are.
**Natural jus, no flour.** Roasted bones, a long, gentle simmer and reduction give body and clarity; flour would dull the beef flavor and turn it into gravy.
**Leftovers become a French dip.** 4 Charles serves a prime rib French dip with Swiss cheese and natural jus; see the make-ahead notes.

substitutions.label: Lactose-free horseradish cream
substitutions.text: Crème fraîche is lower in lactose than cream but not lactose-free. Use 240 g lactose-free sour cream (or lactose-free cream cheese loosened with 2–3 tbsp lactose-free milk). Sour cream is a little tangier and less rich, which suits horseradish well.

substitutions.label: Without vinegar
substitutions.text: Leave out the vinegar: grate the horseradish, wait 2–3 minutes for the heat to develop, then fold it straight into the crème fraîche with the salt and sugar. Without acid the heat isn’t fixed, so it fades over a few hours; make it no more than 2 hours ahead. It tastes rounder and creamier, with less sharpness. Verjus (same amount) is a good acidic alternative that’s milder than vinegar.

substitutions.label: Without wine
substitutions.text: Deglaze the jus pan with water or stock instead of red wine. The jus is slightly less deep and fruity but still excellent.

substitutions.label: Boneless roast
substitutions.text: A 2.5 kg (5½ lb) boneless ribeye roast, tied at 3 cm intervals, works with the same temperatures; start checking it about 1 hour earlier, as it cooks faster without bones.

substitutions.label: Fresh horseradish
substitutions.text: If you can’t find fresh root, use 80 g (⅓ cup) prepared horseradish, squeezed dry, and leave out the vinegar (it already contains some). It is less aromatic and less fiery.

substitutions.label: 4 Charles Cut (Gorgonzola aged)
substitutions.text: The restaurant also serves a Gorgonzola-aged prime rib. We haven’t attempted it: the aging method isn’t published and isn’t safe to improvise at home.

mistakes.problem: A thick gray band under the crust
mistakes.fix: The oven was too hot. Roast at 110°C (225°F), checked with an oven thermometer, and sear only at the end.
Pull it by temperature, not time, at 50°C for medium-rare, and check in more than one spot.
The salt crust steams the surface; always finish with 6–10 minutes in a very hot oven after resting.
Leave the cut faces out of the crust and keep the dry brine at about 0.8% when using a crust.
Simmer gently and never boil, skim often, and defat both the stock and the roast drippings.
Reduce it further; meaty bones with plenty of connective tissue (short rib, oxtail, neck) give the most body.
Use fresh root grated just before mixing, wait 2 minutes before adding acid, and grate finely to release more of the pungent compounds.
Rest the roast 30–60 minutes before the final sear, and slice with a sharp knife in long strokes.

makeAhead: Jus: make up to 4 days ahead and refrigerate (lift off the fat cap once cold), or freeze up to 3 months; finish with the roast drippings on the day.
Horseradish cream with vinegar: up to 2 days ahead, covered, in the refrigerator. Without vinegar, make it no more than 2 hours ahead.

Holding: after the crust comes off, the roast can wait, loosely tented, in a warm spot in the kitchen for up to 1½ hours instead of 30–60 minutes; heat the oven to its maximum during the last 20 minutes, then give it the final blast. It loses a few degrees but the sear and hot jus bring it back.
Leftovers: wrap tightly and refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat slices gently in barely simmering jus for 30–60 seconds; microwaving or high heat turns them gray and tough.

Prime rib French dip: slice cold leftover prime rib very thin, warm it in barely simmering jus for 30 seconds, and pile it onto split, lightly toasted French rolls. Top with sliced Swiss cheese, broil 1 minute until melted, and serve with a small bowl of hot jus for dipping.

verified: **Salt-crusted and roasted low and slow.** World’s 50 Best describes 4 Charles’s prime rib as salt-crusted USDA prime rib, roasted low and slow, served with beef jus and horseradish cream; Time Out also calls it slow-roasted and salt-crusted.

**Thick or thin, same roast.** The menu offers the Chicago Cut (generous, center cut), the English Cut (thin sliced and delicate) and a double-cut, bone-in King Cut, all with natural beef jus and horseradish cream.
recommended: **Gentle heat for edge-to-edge pink:** at 110°C the outside of the roast is barely hotter than the inside, so the whole eye reaches medium-rare with almost no gray band. A high-heat roast overcooks the outer few centimeters before the center is ready.

**Season days ahead, brown at the end.** A 24–72 hour uncovered dry brine seasons deep into the meat and dries the surface; the salt crust then keeps the exterior moist and gentle, and a final blast after resting gives the browning and crisp fat that the crust prevents.
**A natural jus that tastes of beef:** roasted bones, a gentle simmer with no flour and the roast’s own drippings give a clear, savory jus that seasons each slice rather than coating it like gravy.

recipe.why: 4 Charles publishes no recipe, but its menu and press coverage are consistent about the essentials: USDA prime rib that is salt-crusted and roasted low and slow, carved in thick and thin cuts, served with natural beef jus and horseradish cream. We built a home method around those facts with a probe thermometer and specific temperatures. A long dry brine handles the seasoning, the salt crust supplies its gentle, moist heat, and a final sear after resting replaces the browning the crust prevents. The jus is a classic flour-free reduction of roasted bones. The temperatures, timings and crust formula are our own reasoning, not the restaurant’s.

confirmed: 4 Charles Prime Rib is at 4 Charles St in the West Village, from Hogsalt and Brendan Sodikoff (search results).

The menu lists Roast Prime Rib — Chicago Cut: generous, center cut, $104.99; English Cut: thin sliced and delicate; King Cut: double cut, bone-in; and 4 Charles Cut: Gorgonzola-aged prime rib with horseradish cream and natural beef jus (official menu, seen in search results).
Salt-crusted USDA prime rib, roasted low and slow and served with beef jus and horseradish cream (World’s 50 Best Discovery); slow-roasted and salt-crusted (Time Out).
The menu also offers a Prime Rib French Dip with Swiss cheese and natural jus, $39.99 (official menu).
Sides include creamed spinach with blue cheese and sweet onions, and buttery mashed potatoes with roasted garlic and chicken jus (official menu).
inferred: An oven temperature of about 110°C (225°F) and a medium-rare pull temperature of 50°C (122°F).
A dry brine before the salt crust, and an egg-white salt crust over the fat cap.
A final high-heat sear after resting.
A natural jus made from roasted bones, stock and drippings, without flour.
Horseradish cream made from fresh horseradish and crème fraîche.
uncertain: The restaurant’s roasting temperature, time, crust recipe and whether it dry-brines.
Whether the meat is seared or finished after roasting.
Portion weights for each cut, and how the Gorgonzola aging is done.

simple.subtitle: Dry-brined two-bone rib roast, slow-roasted and seared, with quick pan jus and horseradish sour cream
simple.description: The same low-and-slow method and final sear on a smaller two-bone roast, dry-brined overnight instead of salt-crusted, with a quick jus from the drippings and good boxed stock and a stir-together horseradish cream. Most of the time is unattended oven time.

items.item: 2-bone standing rib roast, small end (4½ lb), or a 1.6 kg (3½ lb) boneless ribeye roast, tied
fine sea salt, about 1% of the weight (3⅓ tsp; or 2½ tbsp Diamond Crystal kosher salt); 16 g (2⅔ tsp) for the boneless roast
small onion or 2 shallots, finely chopped
neutral oil or beef fat from the pan (1 tbsp)
good low-sodium boxed beef stock (3 cups)
Pan drippings from the roast, defatted
1 tbsp snipped chives and a pinch of salt

equipment: Sharp slicing knife and carving board

steps.title: Dry-brine overnight
steps.text: The day before (or up to 3 days ahead), pat the roast dry, season it all over with the salt and pepper, and refrigerate uncovered on a rack over a plate or tray.
steps.cue: A dry, darkened surface the next day. If you only have a few hours, salt it 2 hours ahead and leave it at room temperature; it will be seasoned less deeply.

steps.title: Roast low
steps.text: Heat the oven to 110°C (225°F). Set the roast bone side down on the rack in the roasting pan, insert the probe into the center of the eye, and roast until it reads 50°C (122°F) for medium-rare, about 3–3½ hours for a 2 kg bone-in roast (2½–3 hours boneless).
steps.cue: Go by the probe, not the clock: rare 46°C (115°F), medium 54°C (130°F).

steps.title: Make the horseradish cream
steps.text: Stir the horseradish, sour cream, chives and salt together and refrigerate.
steps.cue: A thick, sharp cream. Add more horseradish if you like it hotter.

steps.title: Rest the roast
steps.text: Take out the roast, tent it loosely with foil and rest 30 minutes. Turn the oven to its highest setting, 260–290°C (500–550°F).
steps.cue: The temperature rises only 1–3°C during the rest.

steps.title: Make the quick jus
steps.text: Pour the drippings into a fat separator or cup and spoon off the fat. In the saucepan, cook the onion in 1 tbsp of the fat over medium heat for 4 minutes until browned. Add the wine (if using) and boil 1 minute, then add the stock, thyme and defatted drippings. Boil steadily until reduced by about half, 12–15 minutes, strain, and taste for salt.
steps.cue: A savory, glossy jus that tastes of beef rather than of stock. If it’s thin, reduce a few minutes more.

steps.title: Sear in a very hot oven
steps.text: Return the roast to the very hot oven for 6–10 minutes, until the outside is deep brown and the fat is sizzling.
steps.cue: A crackling, browned crust. No second rest is needed.

steps.title: Carve and serve
steps.text: Cut the bones away, then slice thick (about 3 cm / 1¼ in) or thin (5 mm / ¼ in) across the grain. Serve with hot jus spooned over and the horseradish cream on the side.
steps.cue: Even pink from edge to edge, with a thin brown crust.

tips: Dry-brine at least overnight, uncovered: it seasons deeply and dries the surface for a better crust.
Cook to temperature with a probe thermometer; the clock is only a guide.
Rest before the final sear, so you can carve straight away.
Check your oven with an oven thermometer at low settings.
Low-and-slow roasting gives few drippings, so good stock carries the jus.
simplified: **No salt crust:** the dry brine alone seasons the meat; the outer layer is a touch less moist, but the crust is crisper and there’s nothing to crack off.
**A smaller 2-bone or boneless roast** cooks about 1–1½ hours faster and suits 4 people.
**Quick jus from drippings and boxed stock** in 20 minutes: lighter in body and less deeply roasted than a jus from roasted bones.
**Prepared horseradish and sour cream:** less fragrant and fiery than freshly grated root, and prepared horseradish contains vinegar (see substitutions).

substitutions.label: Lactose-free
substitutions.text: Use lactose-free sour cream in the horseradish cream; the result is almost identical.

substitutions.label: Without vinegar
substitutions.text: Prepared horseradish is preserved in vinegar. Instead, finely grate 40 g fresh horseradish root, wait 2–3 minutes, and fold it into the sour cream; serve within 2 hours, as its heat fades without acid.

substitutions.label: Without wine
substitutions.text: Skip the wine and add 120 ml more stock; the jus is slightly less deep.

makeAhead: The jus keeps 4 days refrigerated; the horseradish cream (with prepared horseradish) keeps 2 days.
Leftovers keep 4 days; warm thin slices in barely simmering jus for a French dip on toasted rolls with melted Swiss cheese.
